landmarks.name: Salar de Uyuni
landmarks.writeup: The world's largest salt flat, known for its vast, reflective surface and unique landscapes.

wiki.extract: Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world, with an area of approximately 10,582 square kilometres (4,086 mi2). It is situated in southwestern Bolivia, within the Daniel Campos Province of the Potosí Department, near the crest of the Andes Mountains, at an elevation of 3,656 m (11,995 ft) above sea level.

landmarks.name: Lake Titicaca
landmarks.writeup: The highest navigable lake in the world, shared with Peru, rich in cultural significance.

wiki.extract: Lake Titicaca is a large lake in the Andes mountains on the border of Bolivia and Peru. It is often called the highest navigable lake in the world. It is often listed as a freshwater lake, though its waters are slightly brackish. Titicaca is the largest lake in South America, both in terms of the volume of water and surface area. It is the 18th largest lake in the world. It has a surface elevation of 3,812 m (12,507 ft).

landmarks.name: Tiwanaku
landmarks.writeup: An ancient archaeological site featuring ruins of a pre-Incan civilization.

wiki.extract: Tiwanaku is a Pre-Columbian archaeological site in western Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, about 70 kilometers from La Paz, and it is one of the largest sites in South America. Surface remains currently cover around 4 square kilometers and include decorated ceramics, monumental structures, and megalithic blocks. It has been conservatively estimated that the site was inhabited by 10,000 to 20,000 people in AD 800.

landmarks.name: Madidi National Park
landmarks.writeup: A biodiverse rainforest park in the Amazon basin, home to many rare species.

wiki.extract: Madidi National Park is a national park in the upper Amazon River basin in Bolivia. It was established in 1995 with a total land area of 18,958 km2. Together with the nearby protected areas Manuripi-Heath and Apolobamba and the Manu Biosphere Reserve (Peru), Madidi is part of one of the largest protected areas in the world.

landmarks.name: Potosí
landmarks.writeup: A historic city famous for its silver mines and colonial architecture.

wiki.extract:
Potosí, known as Villa Imperial de Potosí in the colonial period, is the capital city and a municipality of the Department of Potosí in Bolivia. It is one of the highest cities in the world at a nominal 4,067 m (13,343 ft). 
Diego Huallpa, an indigenous prospector, is traditionally credited with the discovery of the Cerro Rico in 1545, which led to the founding and rapid growth of Potosí due to its extraordinary silver wealth.

cultural_events.name: Carnaval de Oruro
cultural_events.writeup: A UNESCO-recognized festival featuring traditional dances, music, and costumes.

wiki.extract:
The Carnival of Oruro is a religious and cultural festival in Oruro, Bolivia.
Originally an indigenous festival, the celebration later was transformed to incorporate a Christian ritual around the Virgin of Socavón.
The carnival is one of UNESCO's Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

cultural_events.name: Alasitas Festival
cultural_events.writeup: A fair where people buy miniature versions of items they wish to acquire.

wiki.extract: The largest Alasitas fair is an annual month-long cultural event starting on 24 January in La Paz, Bolivia. It honours Ekeko, the Aymara god of abundance, and is noted for the giving of miniature items. Other fiestas and ferias throughout Bolivia incorporate alasitas into religious observances: The Fiesta of the Virgin of Copacabana and the Fiesta of the Virgin of Urkupiña, for example.

cultural_events.name: Fiesta de la Virgen de la Candelaria
cultural_events.writeup: A religious festival celebrated with music, dance, and processions.

wiki.extract: The dance of the Tobas is a Bolivian folkoric dance created in the city of Oruro in the early 20th century. Currently, it is performed in important festivals such as the Carnaval de Oruro and the Fiesta del Gran Poder. Its origin is urban and it holds little relation to the Toba people, although this tribe was the main inspiration for its creation.

food_writeup: Bolivian cuisine features staples like potatoes, corn, and quinoa, with dishes such as salteñas (savory pastries), pique macho (spicy meat dish), and api (a traditional hot corn drink).
brief_history: Bolivia gained independence from Spain in 1825. It has a rich indigenous heritage and has experienced political and social changes, including struggles over natural resources and indigenous rights.

commentary.inflation_management: Bolivia was Latin America's low-inflation outlier for most of the period, an artifact of the fixed exchange rate (6.86 bolivianos per dollar since 2011) and heavy fuel subsidies rather than of monetary credibility. Inflation spiked to 14% in 2008 and 9.9% in 2011 on food and commodity prices, then stayed under 6% from 2012 through 2024, including 1.8% in 2019, 0.7% in 2021, and 2.6% in 2023. The model broke in 2024-25: dollar and fuel shortages, a parallel exchange rate far above the official peg, and subsidy cuts pushed inflation to 5.1% in 2024 and a projected 19.5% in 2025 - the highest in the series. With international reserves reportedly near exhaustion and the peg undefended in practice, the new government inherits an exchange-rate regime in name only.
commentary.debt_management: Bolivia entered the period unusually strong: debt fell from 48.6% of GDP in 2006 to 30.5% in 2011 on HIPC-era relief and the gas boom. It then climbed almost every year as gas revenues faded and deficits became structural: 31.8% in 2014, 48.9% in 2019, 67.5% in 2020 on COVID, 78.3% in 2023, 83.2% in 2024, and a projected 84.8% in 2025. The headline ratio understates the strain, since the central bank financed deficits by drawing down reserves while the official peg masked the monetary expansion. GDP in dollar terms barely grew from $39.3bn in 2014 to a projected $64.3bn in 2025, so the debt burden is real, not a denominator illusion. The next administration faces the classic choice: fiscal consolidation and devaluation, or continued reserve depletion.

key_events.event: Evo Morales took office; gas nationalization funded a decade of high spending.
Commodity super-cycle: gas and mineral revenues drove rapid GDP growth and debt reduction.
Oil and gas price collapse ended the boom; fiscal surpluses turned to persistent deficits.
Disputed October election led to Morales's resignation in November and an interim government.
COVID-19; Luis Arce (Morales's former economy minister) won the October election.
Attempted military coup in June amid dollar and fuel shortages; economic crisis deepened.
Rodrigo Paz won the October runoff with 54.5%, ending nearly 20 years of MAS rule; inflation projected at 19.5%.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Bolivia is at a genuine inflection point: the gas-and-subsidy model is exhausted and the October 2025 election handed a center-right government a mandate for change. The base case is a painful but necessary adjustment - devaluation, subsidy reform, and IMF engagement - that restores stability within a few years and opens lithium and mineral investment. The risk is that adjustment without a social cushion replays the unrest of 2019, and that depleted reserves force a disorderly rather than orderly transition. Watch the exchange rate: a unified, credible FX regime is the single best predictor of whether the new era sticks.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
